content: The periodic table, in its large version, provides a comprehensive representation of the chemical elements. It includes the symbol, atomic number, and standard atomic weight for each element. The periodic table is a tabular arrangement designed to display the chemical elements systematically. While earlier versions of such a table existed, the invention of the modern periodic table is widely attributed to the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev's primary goal was to demonstrate recurring, or periodic, trends in the properties of the elements. Over time, the structure of the periodic table has been refined and expanded as new elements have been discovered and as theoretical models have evolved to better explain chemical behavior. Today, the periodic table is an indispensable tool in the field of chemistry, offering a highly effective framework for classifying, organizing, and comparing the diverse chemical behaviors of elements. Beyond chemistry, the periodic table has also found significant applications in physics, biology, engineering, and various industrial fields. As of January 27, 2008, the standard periodic table includes 117 confirmed elements. Although element 118 has been synthesized, element 117 has not yet been confirmed. For elements with atomic masses listed in brackets, the value represents the atomic mass of the most stable isotope unless it is an integer, in which case it refers to the mass number of the most stable isotope. In all other cases, the value reflects the relative atomic mass based on common terrestrial composition, as defined by the Atomic Weights of the Elements 2001. This value includes its uncertainty, which is indicated in parentheses, and accounts for local variability around the Earth, typically within 0.00007 atomic mass units. For certain elements that have not yet been discovered, the atomic mass is only an estimate.
